211.title: Caesar's coin (Mark 12:13–17)
211.hook: whose image is on it? give Caesar his, and God what is God's
211.howItsDone: Christians often quote "render to Caesar" in discussions of faith, taxes and government, and many teach from Genesis 1:27 that every person bears God's image and so deserves dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the vineyard tenants, and your line was the rejected stone. Who did you notice that others overlook? Day two hundred eleven.

Next come some Pharisees together with some Herodians, supporters of Herod's family, which ruled with Rome's blessing. Normally these two groups didn't agree on much. Mark says they were sent to catch him in his words. They start with flattery, thick as honey. Teacher, we know you're honest, you don't care what anyone thinks, you teach God's way truly. And then the question: is it lawful to pay the tax to Caesar, or not? Should we pay, or shouldn't we? It's the perfect trap. Say yes, and the crowd, who hate the Roman tax, will see a collaborator. Say no, and the Herodians have a rebel to report to Rome. There's no safe answer. So Jesus asks for something small.
screen: `AN ODD PAIR, SENT TO CATCH HIM.` → `FLATTERY, THICK AS HONEY.` → `SHALL WE GIVE, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, he says: "bring me a penny, that I may see it." The penny was a denarius, a silver coin, about a day's wage. And notice: he has to ask for one. He doesn't carry it. They do, right there in the temple courts. Then the question: "Whose is this image and superscription?" Image and inscription. And they answer: "Caesar's." The coins of that emperor, Tiberius, carried his face, and many carried words calling him the son of the divine Augustus. Then the line: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And Mark says they marveled at him. Here's what's hiding in it. The word for image is the same idea as the first chapter of the Bible, where God makes human beings in his own image. So if a coin with Caesar's face on it belongs to Caesar, give it back to him. But what has God's image stamped on it? You do. Every person does. Caesar can have the coin. God asks for the person. Christians have drawn many practical conclusions from this line. Some hear a clear line between church and state. Others hear a limit on what any government can claim. Many Christians pay their taxes and also say that conscience belongs to God alone. What they share is the picture: a face on a coin, and a face in the mirror, and the question of whose each one is.
screen: `BRING ME A PENNY.` · `WHOSE IMAGE IS THIS?` · `GIVE CAESAR WHAT BEARS HIS FACE.` · `YOU BEAR GOD'S IMAGE.` · then, large: `RENDER TO CAESAR THE THINGS THAT ARE CAESAR'S, AND TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask whose image you bear. Settle, and breathe. If you have a coin or a bill nearby, hold it and look at the face on it. If not, picture one. Then think about your own face, the one you'll see in the mirror tonight. The Bible says it carries God's image. Let that sit for a minute. What in your day belongs to Caesar, to the bills and the job and the rules? And what belongs only to God? If you pray, you can offer that part back. The bell holds the time.
Caesar's coin. A denarius with the emperor's face: give it to Caesar, and give to God what bears God's image.
Your line: you bear god's image. Today, when you see someone's face, remember whose image it carries, and treat them that way. Day two hundred eleven.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus says pay your taxes.
what it means: the coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back; you bear God's image, so give yourself to God.
what a scholar hears: eikōn, as in the Greek of Genesis 1:27, and a denarius of Tiberius calling him son of the divine Augustus.

212.title: Whose wife? (Mark 12:18–27)
212.hook: a trick question about seven brothers; he is God not of the dead but of the living
212.howItsDone: Christians confess "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed, and at Christian funerals this hope is often spoken over the grave; many remember the dead by name in prayer, especially on All Saints' and All Souls' Days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a coin with Caesar's face on it, and your line was you bear god's image. Whose face did you see differently? Day two hundred twelve.

Another group steps up with another trap. This time it's the Sadducees, and Mark tells us straight away what they believed: they say there is no resurrection. They come with a story built to make the whole idea look ridiculous. The Law of Moses said that if a man died without children, his brother should marry the widow, so the family line would go on. So, they say: there were seven brothers. The first marries and dies, no children. The second marries her, and dies. The third. All seven. Last of all, the woman dies too. Here's the punchline, in the King James Bible: "In the resurrection therefore, when they shall rise, whose wife shall she be of them?" You can almost hear them smirking.
screen: `THE SADDUCEES: NO RESURRECTION.` → `SEVEN BROTHERS, ONE WIFE.` → `WHOSE WIFE SHALL SHE BE?`

segments.voice: Jesus doesn't laugh along. He says: "Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?" Two mistakes. First, you're imagining the life to come as this life stretched out, with the same arrangements. When the dead rise, he says, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven. God's power isn't limited to making more of the same. And notice the woman: in their story she's only a puzzle, passed down a line of brothers. He refuses to play. Second, the scriptures. The Sadducees leaned on the five books of Moses, so that's where he goes. At the burning bush, God tells Moses: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Not I was. I am. Abraham had been dead for centuries. And then the line: "He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living." If God is still their God, they are still his. Jews in Jesus's day debated this. The Pharisees taught the resurrection of the dead, and many Jews still praise God, in daily prayer, as the one who gives life to the dead. On this question, Jesus stood with the Pharisees. Today's word, resurrection, is anastasis in Greek: literally standing up again. Christians of every church confess it in the old creeds, the resurrection of the body. How it will be, the text doesn't say. That it will be, Jesus is sure: God is the God of the living.
screen: `YOU KNOW NOT THE SCRIPTURES.` · `NOT MORE OF THE SAME.` · `I AM, NOT I WAS.` · `ANASTASIS: STANDING UP AGAIN.` · then, large: `HE IS NOT THE GOD OF THE DEAD, BUT THE GOD OF THE LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone you've lost, with hope. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind. A grandparent, a friend, a parent, even a pet if that's where your heart goes. Picture them as they were at their best. Don't rush past the ache if it's there. If you believe, you can hold them before the God of the living, and let hope sit next to the grief. If you're not sure what you believe, simply give thanks that they were, and still are, part of you. The bell holds the time.
Resurrection. In Greek, anastasis, standing up again. Jesus says God is the God of the living.
Your line: god of the living. Today, say the name of someone you've lost out loud, to someone who knew them, or just to yourself. Day two hundred twelve.

213.title: The greatest commandment (Mark 12:28–34)
213.hook: love God with all you are, and your neighbor as yourself
213.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize the two great commandments, and some churches read them aloud in worship as a summary of the Law; Jews recite the Shema morning and evening, and Christians often note that Jesus prayed it too.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was resurrection, standing up again, and your line was god of the living. Whose name did you say out loud? Day two hundred thirteen.

After a string of traps, a different kind of person walks up. A scribe, an expert in the Law, has been standing at the edge of the crowd listening to all these arguments, and he's noticed that Jesus answered well. So he asks a real question, not a trick. In the King James Bible: "Which is the first commandment of all?" It's a big question. Later Jewish tradition counted six hundred and thirteen commandments in the Law of Moses. Teachers loved to ask which one held all the others together. If you had to put your whole life's faith on one index card, what would you write? Jesus doesn't need to think about it. He starts with a word every Jewish child in that crowd would have known by heart.
screen: `A SCRIBE, LISTENING.` → `A REAL QUESTION, NOT A TRAP.` → `WHICH IS THE FIRST?`

segments.voice: Here's his answer: "The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment." Hear, in Hebrew, is Shema. It's the first word of Deuteronomy chapter six, and the name of the prayer built around it. Jesus was a Jew, and he would have said the Shema every morning and evening, as observant Jews still do today. It's written on the small scroll many Jewish families fix to their doorposts. So when he's asked for the heart of it all, he begins with the prayer at the heart of his own people's life. Notice he doesn't stop at one. He adds a second, from Leviticus: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Two loves, never meant to be separated: love of God, and love of the person next to you. And then something rare happens. The scribe agrees, warmly. Well said, teacher. Loving God and neighbor matters more than all the burnt offerings and sacrifices. And Jesus, seeing he answered wisely, says: "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God." After that, Mark says, nobody dared ask him anything more. In a chapter full of traps, the kindest exchange is between Jesus and a scribe. And a small detail: in Hebrew, Deuteronomy lists heart, soul and strength. Mark's version has four, adding mind. All of you, every part, nothing held back.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `THE PRAYER JESUS SAID DAILY.` · `LOVE GOD, AND YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `A SCRIBE WHO AGREES.` · then, large: `THOU ART NOT FAR FROM THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say both commandments, slowly. Settle, and breathe. If you like, say them aloud or in your head, one phrase per breath. Hear, O Israel. The Lord our God is one Lord. Love the Lord your God with all your heart. With all your soul. With all your mind. With all your strength. And love your neighbor as yourself. Then sit with whichever phrase caught you. If you don't pray, you can simply notice which of the two loves feels harder today. The bell holds the time.
Shema. Hebrew for hear, the first word of the prayer Jesus named as the first commandment of all.
Your line: not far from the kingdom. Today, do one thing that joins both loves: something for God that's also good for your neighbor. Day two hundred thirteen.

214.title: The widow's mite (Mark 12:35–44)
214.hook: after warning against showy religion, he points to a widow's two coins
214.howItsDone: Christians often speak of giving their "mite" when offering what little they have, and churches frequently read this story when talking about giving, stressing the cost of a gift rather than its size.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shema and the two great loves. Your line was not far from the kingdom. What did you do that joined both loves? Day two hundred fourteen.

Still teaching in the temple, Jesus warns the crowd about a certain kind of religious show-off. Beware of those, he says, who love to walk around in long robes, and be greeted with respect in the marketplace, and get the best seats in the synagogue and the places of honor at dinners. They devour widows' houses, and for show they make long prayers. Just yesterday a scribe was praised, so this isn't about everyone; it's about a type we all know. Then Jesus sits down across from the temple treasury, where people drop in their offerings, and he watches. Rich people come by and put in large amounts. Then a poor widow walks up, and drops in two tiny copper coins. Nobody else would have noticed.
screen: `BEWARE THE LONG ROBES.` → `HE SITS AND WATCHES.` → `TWO TINY COINS.`

segments.voice: Jesus calls his disciples over. Look at her. In the King James Bible: "this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living." More. Not in amount. In what it cost. The rich gave from what was left over. She gave from what she needed to eat. The coins were the smallest there were. In Greek, lepton means something like a thin little one, and Mark translates for his readers: two of them make one quadrans, a small Roman coin the King James calls a farthing. The mite in our title is an old English name for the tiniest coin around. Christians have read this story in two ways, and they fit together. Most often it's a picture of true generosity: God counts the heart and the cost, not the size of the check. It's why people still speak of giving their mite. But some readers notice where Mark put it: right after the warning about people who devour widows' houses. They hear a lament too. Here's a widow giving her last coins to a temple whose leaders are eating up widows. Jesus doesn't stop her, and he honors her. And he also sees the system around her. Either way, the one who noticed her was Jesus. Among all the big givers and long robes, he sat still long enough to see two coins drop, and to know what they meant.
screen: `MORE THAN ALL THE REST.` · `OF THEIR ABUNDANCE; OF HER WANT.` · `LEPTON: THE THINNEST COIN.` · `PRAISE, AND A LAMENT.` · then, large: `SHE OF HER WANT DID CAST IN ALL THAT SHE HAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit across from the treasury. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last week. Who gave something quietly, at real cost, without anyone noticing? The coworker who covered a shift. A parent who went without. The neighbor who dropped off soup. Picture them, and what it cost them. Let yourself be the one who notices. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. The bell holds the time.
The widow's mite. Two of the smallest coins, and Jesus says she gave more than all of them.
Your line: she gave all she had. Today, tell one quiet giver that you saw what they did, and that it mattered. Day two hundred fourteen.

215.title: Not one stone (Mark 13:1–13)
215.hook: he foretells the temple's fall and hard times: don't be anxious what to say
215.howItsDone: Christians facing trials or hard conversations often pray for the Holy Spirit's help in what to say, taking comfort from this promise, and many churches read Mark 13 in Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow's two coins, and your line was she gave all she had. Who did you tell that you'd noticed? Day two hundred fifteen.

Picture a first-time visitor to a huge city, neck craned back, staring at the skyline. That's one of the disciples as they walk out of the temple. In the King James Bible: "Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!" And he had a point. King Herod had rebuilt the temple on a massive scale, and some of its stones were bigger than a truck. You can still see some of the giant stones of its outer wall in Jerusalem today. And Jesus says: "Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down." Later they sit on the Mount of Olives, looking across the valley at the temple glowing in the sun, and four of them ask him quietly: when? And how will we know?
screen: `WHAT STONES! WHAT BUILDINGS!` → `NOT ONE STONE UPON ANOTHER.` → `WHEN? HOW WILL WE KNOW?`

segments.voice: What follows is the longest speech Jesus gives in Mark, all of chapter thirteen. Scholars sometimes call it the little apocalypse. It's full of strange images, and Christians read it in several ways; we'll take it in pieces over three days. Today, the beginning. He doesn't give them a date. He gives them warnings. Watch out that no one deceives you. Many will come claiming to be him. You'll hear of wars and rumors of wars; don't be troubled. Earthquakes, famines: these, he says, are the beginnings of sorrows, a word for birth pains. Painful, but not the end. Then it gets personal. You'll be handed over to councils, beaten, brought before governors and kings because of me. Families will split. And right there, in the middle of the frightening part, the most tender line: "take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost." Don't rehearse it. Don't lie awake scripting it. You won't be alone. History adds a hard footnote. In the year 70, during a Jewish revolt, Roman armies destroyed the temple. It has never been rebuilt, and Jews mourn its loss to this day, especially on a fast called Tisha B'Av. Many scholars think Mark was written close to that time. And the section ends: he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. Not the one with the best speech. The one who keeps going.
screen: `NO DATE, JUST WARNINGS.` · `THE BEGINNING OF BIRTH PAINS.` · `DON'T SCRIPT IT BEFOREHAND.` · `THE TEMPLE FELL IN THE YEAR 70.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT YE THAT SPEAK, BUT THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set down one worry about tomorrow. Settle, and breathe. What conversation, meeting or moment are you already rehearsing in your head? The awkward talk, the interview, the appointment. Notice how many times you've played it through. Now picture setting it down, like a heavy bag at the door, just for these two minutes. It'll still be there. You don't have to carry it right now. If you pray, you can hand it to God and trust what will be given in that hour. The bell holds the time.
Not one stone. The temple's great stones would fall. And in hard times: don't worry beforehand what to say.
Your line: don't worry beforehand. Today, when you catch yourself rehearsing tomorrow, stop, breathe, and come back to now. Day two hundred fifteen.

216.title: The days of distress (Mark 13:14–27)
216.hook: strange apocalyptic images; Christians read them in several ways
216.howItsDone: Christians confess in the Nicene Creed that Christ "will come again"; churches read this chapter especially in Advent, and interpret its images in several ways, from the fall of the temple in 70 to Christ's return at the end of time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not one stone left on another, and your line was don't worry beforehand. Did you catch yourself rehearsing tomorrow? Day two hundred sixteen.

Some parts of the Bible read like a letter from a friend. This part reads like a dream you can't quite explain the next morning. Still on the Mount of Olives, Jesus goes on. When you see a terrible thing standing where it shouldn't, run. Whoever is on the roof, don't go down to fetch anything. Whoever is in the field, don't go back for your coat. Pray it doesn't happen in winter. Then the sky itself seems to come apart: sun darkened, moon gone dim, stars falling. And in the middle of all this, Mark does something he never does anywhere else. He turns to you, the reader, directly, with a little aside in brackets. In the King James Bible: "let him that readeth understand." In other words: pay attention. This is for you.
screen: `LIKE A DREAM YOU CAN'T EXPLAIN.` → `RUN. DON'T GO BACK.` → `LET HIM THAT READETH UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: The terrible thing is called the abomination of desolation, a phrase from the book of Daniel. When Daniel was written, it pointed to a real event: a foreign king, Antiochus, set up a pagan altar in the temple, about two centuries before Jesus. Jews remember the temple's rededication after that at Hanukkah. Jesus borrows the old phrase for a new disaster. Then the cosmic images: the sun darkened, the moon not giving her light, stars falling. Israel's prophets used pictures like these for the fall of empires. And then: they'll see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory, another picture from Daniel, and he'll gather his chosen from the four winds, from one end of the earth to the other. So what does it mean? Christians read it in several ways, and sincere believers land in different places. Many scholars and churches read the first part as about the Roman war and the temple's fall in the year 70. Most Christians read the coming in the clouds as about Christ's return at the end of time, which the old creeds confess: he will come again. Some read nearly all of it as already fulfilled in 70. Others read it as still ahead, a future time of trouble. Mark doesn't settle it, but he keeps coming back to two things. Don't be deceived by people with confident timelines. And later in this same speech, a promise: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away." Whatever the images mean, the speaker's words are meant to be the one steady thing when everything else shakes.
screen: `DANIEL'S ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION.` · `A SKY COMING APART.` · `THE SON OF MAN IN THE CLOUDS.` · `SEVERAL READINGS, ONE PROMISE.` · then, large: `MY WORDS SHALL NOT PASS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read slowly, without fear. Settle, and breathe. Take one line and let it be the steady thing: heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. Breathe in on the first half. Out on the second. If frightening pictures come, from this chapter, or the news, or your own worries, notice them, and come back to the line. You don't have to decode anything today. If you pray, you can rest your fear in that promise. The bell holds the time.
The days of distress. Strange images of flight and falling stars, which Christians read in several ways, around one steady promise.
Your line: my words won't pass away. Today, when a scary headline grabs you, read it slowly, breathe, and hold on to something that lasts. Day two hundred sixteen.

217.title: Keep awake (Mark 13:28–37)
217.hook: learn from the fig tree; no one knows the hour; watch
217.howItsDone: Many churches read this passage on the first Sunday of Advent, the season of watchful waiting before Christmas, and some Christians keep vigils or pray at fixed hours as a way of keeping awake.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the days of distress, and your line was my words won't pass away. What steady thing did you hold on to? Day two hundred seventeen. The end of a week, and the end of the road to Jerusalem.

Think of the first warm week of spring, when you notice the tree outside your window has gone from bare sticks to a green haze almost overnight. You don't need a calendar to know summer's coming. Jesus uses exactly that picture, and it's a fig tree again. In the King James Bible: "Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When her branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is near." A few days ago a fig tree in leaf meant disappointment. Now tender leaves are a sign of something coming. After a whole chapter of strange and frightening images, he ends with a tree, and a doorkeeper, and one word, the shortest carry you'll ever get.
screen: `A TREE GOES GREEN OVERNIGHT.` → `LEARN A PARABLE OF THE FIG TREE.` → `ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Then the most surprising sentence in the chapter: "But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father." Not even the Son. Christians have thought hard about that line for centuries. Whatever else it means, it ends every attempt to set a date. So what do you do if you can't know when? He tells a tiny story. A man goes on a journey, gives each servant their own work, and tells the doorkeeper to watch. You don't know when the master comes, evening, midnight, cockcrow, or morning. Those are the four watches of the Roman night. And listen: Mark's next chapters will walk through exactly those four. An evening supper. A midnight garden where friends fall asleep. A rooster crowing. A morning trial. Then the final word of the speech: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." In Greek, grēgoreite, keep awake. It's where the name Gregory comes from: the watchful one. Watching isn't staring at the sky. The servants in the story are busy with their own work. It's doing today's work awake. Now look back. This week: Caesar's coin, whose wife, the greatest commandment, a widow's mite, not one stone, the days of distress, and keep awake. And the whole road: back on day two hundred it turned south with a question about marriage. Children in his arms. A rich man walking away. Bartimaeus, a borrowed colt, the temple, a rejected stone. Now the road has reached Jerusalem. Tomorrow, the last days begin.
